content: The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy (2011–2015) by the World Health Organization (WHO) aimed to reduce the number of new leprosy cases with grade-2 disabilities by 35% by the end of the strategy period. This strategy emphasized the importance of early detection and high-quality care within integrated healthcare services. To achieve greater success in leprosy control, it is crucial to establish robust monitoring and evaluation practices within the program. Monitoring is conducted using a set of indicators that assess the impact, effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, and sustainability of leprosy services. These indicators enable before-and-after analyses to evaluate the effects of program interventions. While routine data collection provides adequate information on program progress and performance, it may not sufficiently assess the quality of care indicators. The procedures for collecting epidemiological and disease control data are well-established in earlier guidelines on Leprosy Elimination Monitoring (LEM). This document also includes additional indicators and methodologies tailored to current needs. Leprosy control has made significant progress, particularly in the last decade, due to intensive case detection campaigns, simplified strategies, integrated primary leprosy services, and collaborative efforts with stakeholders. However, leprosy has not been eradicated, as new cases continue to emerge in endemic countries, including high-burden pockets within low-burden nations. Sustaining leprosy control efforts and ensuring equitable access to services in resource-poor settings remain challenging. Multidrug therapy (MDT) has been the cornerstone of leprosy control, but challenges persist in addressing the specific needs of affected individuals and the program. The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy (2011–2015) targeted a 35% reduction in new cases with disabilities by 2015 compared to the 2011 baseline. It highlighted the importance of early detection and quality care in integrated service settings. Routine data collection focuses on progress and performance but often overlooks quality-of-care issues due to complexities in data management. Monitoring the Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy requires well-established concepts and practices of monitoring and evaluation. Monitoring is conducted through a minimum set of indicators that describe leprosy services in terms of impact, effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, and sustainability. These indicators form the basis for evaluating the effects of program interventions. Monitoring should be quick, cost-effective, and program-oriented, involving a continuous flow of information on progress and performance. Special monitoring studies should also be conducted periodically using methods such as surveys, structured interviews, process analysis, and qualitative approaches to provide complementary evidence on program performance. The procedures for collecting information on disease behavior and program performance through indicators are well-established in earlier LEM guidelines. This document extends those guidelines with methodologies, frameworks, and indicators adapted to current needs. These are applied in the field in a standardized manner by monitors in collaboration with national programs and WHO. Monitors collect information to complement routine leprosy information systems, addressing specific issues such as epidemiological trends, intervention impacts, and quality of services. Key indicators include case detection trends, the proportion of females among new cases, child detection trends, and the availability and quality of MDT services. Monitoring exercises should be time-limited, with the complete cycle (from design to reporting) not exceeding four weeks. Selected health facilities should be informed in advance of monitors’ visits to allow for the mobilization of affected individuals. The protocol includes a compendium of indicators with definitions and criteria for focus. Details of procedures for most indicators are available in the LEM guidelines, which can be adapted to local situations. Five new indicators have been added, and sample questionnaires for patient satisfaction, community perception, and perceived stigma are provided in the annexures. It provides a framework for assessing program performance, identifying areas for improvement, and ensuring the sustainability of leprosy control efforts.
